meta.note: Naming drift, mild: Microsoft's overview is now titled simply “Azure Data Lake Storage” — the Gen2 suffix has quietly dropped out of the product name, though Gen2 still describes the generation and Gen1 is referenced only historically. Name left as-is because “Gen2” remains the term learners will meet in job adverts and existing estates; the short line now records the shift. Flag for next pass: this page states Microsoft “doesn't impose any limits on account sizes, file sizes”, which sits awkwardly beside the write-up's “up to 5 PiB per storage account by default”. Not corrected here, because the 5 PiB figure is a storage-account quota documented elsewhere and needs its own source.

name: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2
short: documented now as Azure Data Lake Storage; Gen2 is the generation
oneLiner: Hierarchical, analytics-optimised object storage built on Blob.
whatItIs: ADLS Gen2 is Azure Blob Storage with a hierarchical namespace (HNS) switched on. That one setting is the whole story: instead of flat keys pretending to be folders, ADLS has real directories you can rename, move and secure atomically. It keeps Blob's cheap, durable, unlimited object storage but adds POSIX-style permissions and directory operations that big-data engines expect — so it's the default data lake underneath Synapse, Databricks and Fabric on Azure. Under the hood it's the same storage account and blobs; the HNS flag is what makes it a 'data lake' rather than plain object storage.

inPractice.narrative: Raw events and files land in an ADLS 'bronze' container. A Databricks or Synapse Spark job cleans them into partitioned Parquet/Delta in a 'silver' container. Synapse SQL (dedicated or serverless) then reads those files, and Power BI reads from Synapse. Because ADLS has real directories, teams organise the lake as bronze/silver/gold folders and grant access per-folder — something flat object stores can't do as cleanly.

coreConcepts.detail: The defining feature — real directories with atomic rename/move/delete and per-directory ACLs. Enabled on the storage account at creation; you can't retrofit it easily, so decide up front.
Data lives in a storage account; containers (a.k.a. filesystems) are the top-level grouping, then directories and files below. One account can serve many workloads.
ADLS Gen2 is Blob storage — same access tiers, redundancy and most APIs — plus the DFS (Data Lake) endpoint for filesystem-style operations. Tools speak either the Blob or the DFS endpoint.
Hot, Cool, Cold and Archive trade storage cost against access cost and retrieval latency (Archive is offline and needs a rehydrate). Lifecycle policies move blobs between tiers by age or last-access.
LRS (one datacentre), ZRS (across zones), GRS/RA-GRS (geo-replicated) — you pick the durability/availability vs cost trade-off per account.
Access combines Azure RBAC (coarse, at container/account) with POSIX-style ACLs on directories and files (fine-grained) — the model Spark/Hadoop security expects.

whenToUse: As the data lake under Synapse, Databricks or Microsoft Fabric.
Analytics workloads that need directory operations and per-folder security.
Landing raw data and organising it into bronze/silver/gold medallion layers.
Storing large Parquet/Delta datasets queried by Spark and Synapse SQL.
Cheap retention via Cool/Cold/Archive tiers with lifecycle management.
whenNotToUse: Low-latency key lookups of small records — use Cosmos DB or Table storage.
In-place row updates and transactions — use a database or a Delta/Iceberg table layer on top.
Simple app blob storage with no analytics needs — plain Blob (HNS off) is fine and cheaper to reason about.
A managed NFS/SMB share for legacy apps — use Azure Files.

keyFacts.label: Durability
keyFacts.value: At least 11 nines with LRS; more with ZRS/GRS.

keyFacts.label: Built on
keyFacts.value: Azure Blob Storage + hierarchical namespace (DFS endpoint).

source.quote: Azure Data Lake Storage isn't a dedicated service or account type. Instead, it's implemented as a set of capabilities that you use with the Blob Storage service of your Azure Storage account. Unlock these capabilities by enabling the hierarchical namespace setting.

keyFacts.label: Key feature
keyFacts.value: Real directories with atomic rename/move and POSIX ACLs.

source.quote: Operations such as renaming or deleting a directory become single atomic metadata operations on the directory. … The Azure Data Lake Storage access control model supports both Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) and Portable Operating System Interface for UNIX (POSIX) access control lists (ACLs).

keyFacts.label: Access tiers
keyFacts.value: Hot / Cool / Cold / Archive (Archive is offline, needs rehydrate).

keyFacts.label: Capacity
keyFacts.value: Effectively unlimited; up to 5 PiB per storage account by default.

pricingShape: You pay for: (1) stored GB-month by access tier, with cold tiers cheaper to hold but pricier to read and subject to minimum retention; (2) operations (reads, writes, list) priced per tier; (3) egress out of the region/Azure; and (4) redundancy — ZRS/GRS cost more than LRS. HNS adds small per-transaction overhead but pays for itself in analytics. As always for lakes, colder tiers plus lifecycle rules keep old data cheap, and Parquet + partitioning cut what downstream engines scan.
gotchas: The hierarchical namespace must be enabled at account creation — turning a flat Blob account into ADLS Gen2 later is a migration, not a toggle.
Two endpoints (Blob vs DFS) exist for the same data; some tools/SDKs only speak one — mismatches cause confusing 'not found' errors.
Archive tier is offline: reading needs a rehydrate that can take hours — don't put anything latency-sensitive there.
GRS gives geo-durability but failover/read access has caveats; know whether you have GRS or RA-GRS before relying on secondary reads.
Egress and cross-region reads are billed — keep Synapse/Databricks in the same region as the account.

equivalents.name: Amazon S3
equivalents.note: Flat object store; S3 lacks a true hierarchical namespace (though Mountpoint/S3 features narrow the gap).

equivalents.name: Cloud Storage
equivalents.note: Flat object store like S3; ADLS's real directories are the main conceptual difference.
